title: Project health score template
metaDescription: A project health score template that scores schedule, scope, dependencies, blockers, and throughput against evidence. See how Husn keeps each dimension honest and current.
heroSubheadline: A template gives you a consistent structure for scoring health. The missing piece is the evidence behind each number and a way to keep it current. Husn supplies both.
primaryPain: Most teams start with a health template, fill it in once, and watch it go stale by the second week. The dimensions are sound, but the scores are still a person's best guess on the day, with no evidence pinned to them and no way to tell when the underlying work has moved away from the rating.
painBullets: A blank template scores nothing on its own, so the quality still depends on whoever fills it in.
Each dimension gets a number with no evidence attached, so nobody can question or trust it later.
The scorecard reflects the day it was filled in, not the work as it stands now.
whyHardHeading: Why a template alone is not enough
whyHard: Scoring five or six dimensions honestly for one project takes time, and that time multiplies across a portfolio until corners get cut.
Without evidence in the row, two reviewers score the same project differently and neither can defend their number.
A trend column is only useful if last period's scores were honest, so one soft entry quietly corrupts the whole trend.
howHusnHelps: Husn fills each dimension from real signals in Jira, Slack, and docs, so schedule, scope, dependencies, blockers, and throughput are scored from the work rather than from memory.
Every score carries its evidence in the same row, the slipped date or aging blocker that drove it, so the number can be questioned and defended.
Husn watches each dimension as the work moves and flags a slipping score early, while there is still room to act before it becomes an incident.

items.text: Dependencies dropped from green to amber after an upstream team moved a delivery date by nine days.
Scope grew by four tickets this sprint with no matching change to the schedule rating.
Throughput has held steady, but blockers are aging and will pull the score down if untouched.

briefing.footer: 5 dimensions scored - evidence in every row - refreshed from live work

templateContents: Scored dimensions, covering schedule, scope, dependencies, blockers, and throughput so health is built from concrete parts rather than one overall feeling.
Rating scale, a consistent green, amber, red basis applied the same way to every project for fair comparison.
Evidence column, the specific signal behind each score, such as a slipped date or an aging blocker, so the number can be defended.
Trend, how each dimension moved since the last period, so a slow slide is visible before it turns red.
Owner, the person accountable for each dimension and the next action when it drops.

useCases.title: Standardising scoring
useCases.body: Give every project the same dimensions and the same scale, so health reads the same way wherever you look.

useCases.title: Defensible reviews
useCases.body: Walk into a review with evidence in every row, so each score holds up when someone pushes back on it.

useCases.title: Catching drift early
useCases.body: Watch a single dimension slide period over period and act on it before it drags the whole project red.

faq.q: Can we use our own dimensions?
faq.a: Yes. The five standard dimensions are a starting point, and Husn can score against the categories your organisation already uses.

faq.q: Where does the evidence come from?
faq.a: From the work itself, in Jira, Slack, and docs, so each score in the template points back to a concrete signal rather than an opinion.

faq.q: Does Husn change anything in our tools?
faq.a: No. It reads the work to fill the scorecard and never writes anything back to Jira, Slack, or your documents.

faq.q: How often does the scorecard update?
faq.a: As the underlying work moves, so the scores and the trend reflect the current state rather than the day the template was filled in.

ctaHeadline: Fill the scorecard from the work, not from memory.
ctaText: Connect your projects and Husn will score every dimension with evidence attached, then flag a slipping score early, in about fifteen minutes.

title: Project status indicators
metaDescription: The status indicators that actually signal project health, and how Husn reads them from Jira, Slack, and docs to flag trouble before it becomes an incident.
heroSubheadline: A status light is only as good as the signal behind it. Husn reads the indicators that matter directly from the work, so a change in state shows up as soon as the work changes.
primaryPain: Most status indicators are entered by hand on a cadence, which means they lag the work and reflect the reporter as much as the project. A green light can sit untouched for a week while blockers pile up beneath it, and nobody knows the indicator is wrong until something breaks.
painBullets: Indicators are set manually, so they show how the project felt at the last update, not where it stands now.
A single overall light hides the specific signal underneath, so you cannot tell what is actually wrong.
By the time an indicator flips, the trouble it signals has usually been building for days.
whyHard: Each team interprets red, amber, and green differently, so the same indicator means different things across a portfolio.
Useful indicators come from several places at once, Jira tickets, Slack threads, and documents, and no person watches all three continuously.
An indicator that only flips on a reporting cycle gives you the signal too late to do anything cheap about it.
howHusnHelps: Husn derives each indicator from live signals across Jira, Slack, and docs, so the light reflects the current state of the work rather than the last manual entry.
Behind every indicator sits the specific reason it moved, the aging blocker, the slipped dependency, the quiet scope change, so you act on the cause, not the color.
Husn watches the leading indicators and raises an amber early, catching the slide before it becomes an incident someone has to explain.

items.text: Project Atlas flipped to red after a critical dependency slipped and a blocker passed eight days open.
A status light moved from green to amber as Slack activity on the workstream went quiet for a week.
An indicator still showing green has had no plan update in eleven days, a common precursor to a flip.

briefing.footer: Indicators from live signals - reason behind every change - no manual lag

faq.q: Can teams still set a manual status?
faq.a: Yes, and Husn will show you where the manual status and the work based indicator disagree, which is often the most telling signal.

faq.q: Does Husn write status back into our tools?
faq.a: No. It reads the work to derive the indicators and never writes anything back.

faq.q: How quickly does an indicator change?
faq.a: As soon as the underlying work moves, rather than waiting for the next reporting cycle, so you see the change while it still matters.

title: AI project health analysis
metaDescription: AI project health analysis that reads tickets, messages, and updates, reconciles them, and explains why a project's health is where it is, before issues become incidents.
heroSubheadline: Tickets, messages, and updates each tell part of the story. Husn reads all three, reconciles what they say, and explains the health of a project with the reasons attached.
primaryPain: Project health lives in three places that rarely agree. Jira says one thing, the Slack thread says another, and the written update says a third. Piecing them together by hand is slow, so people fall back on a quick guess, and the guess misses the early signs of trouble that were sitting in the gaps between the tools.
painBullets: Health signals are scattered across tickets, messages, and documents, and no one reads all three together.
Manual analysis is too slow to keep up, so health gets approximated and the approximation drifts from reality.
The earliest signs of trouble usually appear in the disagreement between tools, exactly where a human eye does not look.
whyHardHeading: Why this is hard to do by hand
whyHard: Reconciling Jira, Slack, and docs for one project is tedious, and across a portfolio it simply does not get done consistently.
The signals that matter are often quiet, a thread that went silent or a date that moved without comment, easy to miss in a manual scan.
Doing this analysis only at report time means the read is always a few days behind the work it describes.
howHusnHelps: Husn reads tickets, messages, and updates together, reconciles where they disagree, and produces a health read grounded in all three rather than one.
Every assessment comes with its reasons, the slipped dependency, the aging blocker, the scope change nobody flagged, so the analysis can be checked and acted on.
Husn runs the analysis continuously and surfaces the early signal in the gaps between tools, so a problem is caught before it becomes an incident.

items.text: Jira shows Project Vega on track, but the team Slack went quiet and the last doc update is two weeks old.
A milestone date moved in the plan with no matching message or ticket explaining why.
A workstream rated healthy has three blockers that have aged past a week without comment.

briefing.footer: Tickets, messages, and updates read together - reasons attached - caught early

faq.q: How does it explain its conclusions?
faq.a: Each health read comes with the specific signals behind it, so you can trace the conclusion to a slipped dependency, an aging blocker, or a quiet scope change.

faq.q: Does Husn change anything in our tools?
faq.a: No. It is read only. It analyses the work to assess health and never writes anything back to Jira, Slack, or your docs.

faq.q: How is this different from a status report?
faq.a: A report is a snapshot someone writes. This analysis runs continuously across the source tools and flags the early signs of trouble before a report would catch them.
